summary: This standards-track memo defines an authentication suboption for the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option from RFC 3046. It carries a keyed hash that lets the DHCP server check that relay-added information is genuine and unmodified, and it provides protection against replay.

eli5.summary: When a helper passes your request to a boss, the boss wants proof the helper's note is real. This adds a secret stamp to the note that cannot be faked.

questions: how to authenticate dhcp relay information
what is the dhcp relay authentication suboption

what is the dhcp relay agent information option
how does dhcp replay detection work
subtitle: A keyed hash and replay counter that let a DHCP server and relay agent trust each other's relay-added data.

tldr.problem: Relay agents add information to DHCP messages after the client sent them, and existing DHCP Authentication explicitly excludes that data, so servers cannot be sure it is genuine.
tldr.mechanism: A new Authentication suboption (code 8) of the Relay Agent Information option carries a replay counter and an HMAC-SHA1 keyed hash computed over the whole DHCP message.
tldr.outcome: Servers and relays can check integrity and reject replayed messages, at the cost of extra hashing work and shared keys to configure.

today: RFC 4030 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Relay Agent Information option in RFC 3046.

sections.title: Why Relay Information Needs Protection
sections.content:
DHCP provides IP addresses and configuration for IPv4 clients. A relay agent receives broadcast messages from clients and forwards them to servers as unicast messages. In networks such as DOCSIS data-over-cable and xDSL, it has proven useful for the relay to add information to the message, using the Relay Agent Information option of RFC 3046. Servers often use that information to decide which addresses and parameters a client gets, so it is very important to trust the relay.

DHCP Authentication (RFC 3118) covers only client to server communication, and it explicitly excludes relay-added data because that data is added after the client sends its message. This RFC aims to protect the integrity of relayed messages, provide replay protection, and reuse existing mechanisms such as DHCP Authentication. Relays that want this are configured with the needed parameters. A server that processes the suboption continues with the relay information only if the checksum is valid, and it puts its own Authentication suboption in any response, which the relay tests before forwarding it.
sections.eli5: The helper adds a note to your request after you hand it over, and the boss cannot tell if the note is real. This memo gives the helper a way to sign the note.

sections.title: The Authentication Suboption
sections.content:
The suboption has the code 8. Its fields are Code, Length, Algorithm, a four-bit MBZ field, a four-bit Replay Detection Method (RDM), a 64-bit Replay Detection value, a Relay Identifier and the Authentication Information. The length counts the algorithm, the RDM and all later fields in octets.

The four MBZ bits are reserved: they SHOULD be zero and MUST NOT be used when the suboption is processed. The Algorithm field says how the authentication information was generated, and the RDM says how to interpret the Replay Detection value. The Relay Identifier is for relays that do not set giaddr. The Authentication Information holds algorithm-specific parameters and the checksum, usually a digest of the DHCP packet.

For Algorithm 1 (HMAC-SHA1) the length is 38, and the Authentication Information holds a 32-bit Key ID followed by the 160-bit HMAC-SHA1 value.
sections.eli5: The stamp has labelled boxes: which kind of secret math was used, a page number, who the helper is, and the signature itself.

sections.title: Replay Detection and Relay Identity
sections.content:
The default RDM, value 1, makes the Replay Detection field an increasing counter. The receiver keeps a counter for each sender and rejects any message whose value is less than or equal to the last valid one. Servers MAY identify relays by giaddr or other data in the message, and relays identify servers by source IP address. All implementations MUST support the default RDM. Receivers SHOULD check the replay value before the checksum, because the keyed hash is likely much more expensive. The cost is some run-time state for each sender.

The Relay Identifier field covers the case where a relay adds the option without setting giaddr, so the receiver needs a stable identifier for per-sender state such as the Key ID and counters. A relay that sets giaddr MUST NOT set the field. A relay that does not MAY put in a configured value or one generated from data such as its MAC or IP address, and SHOULD pick a value it can regenerate reliably, for example across reboots.

Servers SHOULD use giaddr to identify the sender if it is set. Otherwise they SHOULD use the Relay ID if it is nonzero. If neither is set, a server MAY use other data or increment an error counter.
sections.eli5: Every note gets a page number that must be bigger than the last one. If an old note is sent again, its page number is too low and it is thrown away.

sections.title: Computing the Keyed Hash
sections.content:
The sender and receiver hash a buffer holding every byte of the DHCP message: the fixed header, the options and the relay agent suboptions. There are three exceptions. The hops field is set to zero because it may change in transit. The giaddr field is set to zero because another relay may set it. The Authentication Information field is set to all zeros because it is the hash's own result. The lengths and all other suboption fields are included.

All implementations MUST support Algorithm 1, HMAC-SHA1. It needs a shared secret key configured at the relay and the server. Each key has a 32-bit Key ID carried in the first 4 bytes of the Authentication Information, followed by the 20-byte hash. The Key ID is purely local configuration and only has to be unique locally, so the RFC defines no meaning for its values.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix the whole message with a shared secret to get a short code. If their codes match, the message was not changed on the way.

sections.title: Sending and Checking Messages
sections.content:
To send, the sender zeroes giaddr and hops, appends the relay agent information option with the Authentication suboption, picks a Replay Detection value (for RDM 1, greater than any value sent before), fills in the Relay ID if needed, the algorithm and, for HMAC-SHA1, the Key ID, and sets the checksum field to zeros. It computes the checksum over the whole message, stores it, restores hops and giaddr, and sends.

The receiver first examines giaddr and the relay option, and uses its configuration to decide whether to expect the suboption. It MUST support a configuration that drops messages lacking a valid relay option and Authentication suboption. If it cannot work out the algorithm, key or RDM, or does not support them, it SHOULD drop the message and MAY notify an administrator or log an error. Receivers MUST discard unsupported RDM values and MUST drop messages with an invalid replay value.

The receiver MUST NOT update its stored counter until the checksum passes. Otherwise an attacker could replay a message with a very high counter and make the receiver reject the sender's real messages. It then zeroes giaddr, hops and the authentication field, recomputes the hash and drops the message on a mismatch. On success it updates the counter and processes the message.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the page number first because that is quick, then checks the signature. It only writes down the new page number once the signature is proven real.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A relay that implements the suboption needs an algorithm number and keys for each server. Relays SHOULD support a setting that adds the suboption to all relayed messages, and use of the suboption SHOULD be disabled by default. They MAY support per-server settings, either a single algorithm and key for all servers or different ones for each. A relay MAY be configured to drop server responses that lack the suboption. When one relay adds the option and passes the message to another relay, such as a layer-2 switch forwarding to an aggregating router that sets giaddr, the second relay MAY verify the message first.

Servers MAY use the same algorithm and key for all relays or configure each relay individually. A server builds its own Authentication suboption for replies instead of echoing the request's. The RFC notes this is a slight variance from RFC 3046.
sections.eli5: Helpers and bosses keep a list of which secret to use with whom. The feature starts switched off, and the boss writes a fresh signature on each reply.

sections.title: Costs and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The protocol adds source authentication and integrity protection between relays and servers, but also computational work and possible latency, since hashes are computed on every send and receive. Because relays are involved when clients reboot, a burst of reboots creates the most messages to process. The RFC gives a cable MSO head-end reboot as an example where the time to serve all clients may increase.

The Key ID is a fixed four bytes, following the DHCP Authentication RFC. Key names, as used by DNS TSIG, would be more flexible and readable, but the RFC prefers a fixed-length ID to keep the relay option small and the encoding simple.

DHCP runs over UDP, so messages can arrive out of order. The replay check will drop late packets and clients will retry, but the sender's hashing work for those messages is wasted. The RFC also points to a companion approach, authenticating relay agent options using IPsec. IPsec may suit deployments where pairwise keys can be managed efficiently, and this suboption may suit those where IPsec is not available or there are many relays and keys. Local administration chooses between them.
sections.eli5: Signing every note takes time, especially when everyone restarts at once. If notes arrive in the wrong order, the late ones are thrown out and the sender has to try again.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA allocated a suboption code in the relay agent option suboption space and created two new number spaces. The Algorithm identifier is a one-byte value: 0 is reserved and 1 is HMAC-SHA1. The RDM identifier is a four-bit value: 0 is reserved and 1 is a monotonically increasing counter. New values are allocated by IETF consensus as defined in RFC 2434.
sections.eli5: Two lists of numbers were set up, one for kinds of secret math and one for ways to count pages. Each list so far has one entry in use.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Counts the algorithm, RDM and all later fields.

fields.desc: Replay Detection Method; 1 is an increasing counter.

fields.name: Replay Detection
fields.desc: Counter value used to detect replayed messages.

fields.name: Relay Identifier
fields.desc: Stable relay identity when giaddr is not set.

fields.desc: The keyed hash over the DHCP message.
